details:
**Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair**
Neruda's most famous collection, published in 1924 when he was 19. It contains twenty numbered love poems followed by a final poem, "The Song of Despair." Almost every question ends by calling Neruda the "Chilean poet" of this book.

**"In you everything sank!"**
The refrain repeated throughout "The Song of Despair," the last poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. The speaker also calls the lost lover a "pit of debris" and a jar that held "infinite tenderness."

**"Tonight I can write the saddest lines"**
The opening line of Poem 20, the second-to-last poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. Examples of the "saddest lines" include "the night wind revolves in the sky and sings" and "She loved me, sometimes I loved her too." The poem also contains the line "Love is so short, forgetting is so long."

**"It is the hour of departure"**
The closing refrain of "The Song of Despair," which opens with "The memory of you emerges from the night around me." In the same poem the speaker calls himself "deserted like the wharves at dawn" and defines the hour of departure as the "hard cold hour which the night fastens to all the timetables."

**Elemental Odes**
Neruda's 1954 collection of short-lined odes to ordinary things. Subjects include the onion, praised as a "heavenly globe, platinum goblet" that can "make us cry without hurting us," as well as tomatoes, which "invade the kitchen," and conger chowder, a dish in which "you may know heaven."

**"Ode to My Socks"**
An ode to a pair of socks knitted for Neruda by Maru Mori. He says they were made from "threads of twilight and goatskin" and compares his feet to "two fish," "two long sharks," "two immense blackbirds," and "two cannons." It ends with the moral that "beauty is twice beauty and what is good is doubly good."

**"Body of a Woman"**
The first poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. It describes the beloved's "white hills, white thighs" and his own "body, savage and peasant, undermining you." The speaker says he was "lonely as a tunnel" and that "to survive I forged you like a weapon."

**Canto General**
Neruda's 1950 epic about the history of the Americas, with sections such as "The Conquistadors" and "The Liberators" and the canto "America, I Do Not Invoke Your Name in Vain." He finished it while hiding from Chile's government, which had outlawed communism. He escaped on horseback across the Andes (described in *The Grapes and the Wind*) and later traveled to Paris on the passport of Guatemalan novelist Miguel Ángel Asturias. He won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**"The Heights of Macchu Picchu"**
A twelve-part poem in *Canto General*, inspired by Neruda's 1943 visit to the Inca ruins in Peru. It begins with the speaker moving "from air to air, as through an empty net." The last section opens "Arise to birth with me, my brother" and asks the dead laborers to "speak through my words and my blood."

**"Ode to the Artichoke"**
An ode in *Elemental Odes* about a "tender hearted" vegetable dressed like a "solitary man of war among these frail vegetables." At the end, a woman named María buys it at the market along with "a pair of shoes, a white cabbage and a bottle of vinegar," then cooks and eats it.

**"White Bee"**
A poem from *Twenty Love Poems* in which the speaker tells a "white bee" that "you buzz in my soul, drunk with honey." It repeats the refrain "Ah you who are silent!" and includes the lines "I am the one without hope, the word without echoes" and "In my barren land you are the final rose."

**"Ode to a Large Tuna in the Market"**
An ode describing a big tuna for sale at a market as a "torpedo from the ocean." Neruda praises it as "the only true machine of the sea: unflawed, undefiled," a creature that "lived through the sea's truth."

**"A Dog Has Died"**
A late Neruda poem mourning his dog, whom he buried in the garden "next to a rusted old machine," adding that "some day I'll join him right there." He remembers the dog as "full of the voltage of the sea's movement." Although he "never believed in any promised heaven," the speaker believes "in a heaven I'll never enter."

**"The United Fruit Company"**
A political poem in *Canto General* attacking the American banana corporation's power over Central America. It opens with "Jehovah" dividing the world among companies like "Coca-Cola Inc." The company "abolished free will," and the dictators it supports are called "damp flies of modest blood and marmalade."

**"Every Day You Play"**
Poem 14 of *Twenty Love Poems*. It opens "every day you play with the light of the universe," and the speaker promises to bring "rustic baskets of kisses." In W. S. Merwin's translation it ends "I want to do with you what spring does with the cherry trees."

**Coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800**
Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans" in Rome on Christmas Day, 800 CE. This is why he is usually called the first Holy Roman Emperor. Shortly before, Charlemagne had protected Leo, whose enemies in Rome had attacked him and accused him of crimes including adultery.

**Einhard**
Einhard was a Frankish scholar at Charlemagne's court who wrote the *Vita Karoli Magni* (Life of Charles the Great), the most important biography of the ruler. He later served Charlemagne's son Louis the Pious. A legend, generally considered apocryphal, says he eloped with one of Charlemagne's daughters.

**Alcuin of York and the Carolingian Renaissance**
Alcuin was an English scholar who headed Charlemagne's palace school at Aachen. He led the "Carolingian Renaissance," a revival of learning and Latin scholarship named for Charlemagne's dynasty. He retired as abbot of St. Martin at Tours, where scribes developed Carolingian minuscule, a clear, standardized script used to copy texts such as the Vulgate Bible and an ancestor of modern lowercase letters.

**Aachen and the Palatine Chapel**
Aachen, in present-day western Germany, was Charlemagne's favored residence and capital, where his scholars gathered. His Palatine Chapel there, an early building with a monumental "westwork" entrance, is now the core of Aachen Cathedral.

**Desiderius and the conquest of the Lombards (Siege of Pavia)**
Desiderius was the last king of the Lombards in northern Italy. Charlemagne first married Desiderius's daughter (often called Desiderata) for an alliance, then repudiated her and married Hildegard. He besieged and captured the Lombard capital of Pavia in 773–774, took the Iron Crown of Lombardy, and became King of the Lombards.

**Pepin the Short and the Donation of Pepin**
Charlemagne was the son of Pepin the Short, the first Carolingian king of the Franks, and the grandson of Charles Martel, "the Hammer." In the "Donation of Pepin," Pepin granted Italian lands taken from the Lombard king Aistulf to the papacy. Charlemagne confirmed this donation during a visit to Rome while fighting the Lombards. He became sole ruler after his brother Carloman died.

**Massacre of Verden**
In 782, during the Saxon Wars, Charlemagne ordered the execution of about 4,500 Saxon prisoners at Verden, also called the "Bloody Verdict of Verden." It was the most notorious act of his long, brutal campaign to conquer and Christianize the pagan Saxons.

**Battle of Roncevaux Pass and *The Song of Roland***
In 778, after a failed siege of Zaragoza in Spain, Charlemagne's retreating rear guard was ambushed by Basques in the Roncevaux (Roncesvalles) Pass in the Pyrenees. Einhard records it as his only major defeat. The death of the commander Roland there became the subject of the Old French epic *The Song of Roland*.

**Treaty of Verdun**
Signed in 843, this treaty divided Charlemagne's empire among his three grandsons, the sons of Louis the Pious: Lothair I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald. The split roughly anticipated the later realms of France and Germany.

**Widukind and the Irminsul**
Widukind was the leader of Saxon resistance against Charlemagne during the decades-long Saxon Wars. Early in the conflict Charlemagne destroyed the Irminsul, a sacred Saxon pillar or tree. The wars ended with Widukind's submission and baptism.

**Harun al-Rashid and the elephant Abul-Abbas**
The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne diplomatic gifts, including an elephant named Abul-Abbas and an elaborate water clock. The exchange reflected friendly relations between the two rulers.

**Spanish March**
Charlemagne created the Spanish March as a buffer zone between his empire and the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba in Spain. It covered the area between the Pyrenees and the Ebro River, and parts of it later developed into Catalonia.

**Missi dominici**
The *missi dominici* ("envoys of the lord") were royal agents Charlemagne sent out, usually in pairs of a cleric and a lay noble. They inspected local administration, enforced his decrees, and reported abuses by local officials.

**Paul the Deacon and the *History of the Lombards***
Paul the Deacon was a Lombard monk and scholar who spent time at Charlemagne's court. He is best known for the *Historia Langobardorum* (History of the Lombards), a major source on the Lombard people in Italy.

**Capitulary for the Jews**
This set of regulations, attributed to Charlemagne, concerned Jews in his realm. Among its harsh provisions were bans on Jews engaging in moneylending and related transactions. Capitularies were the legislative decrees through which Carolingian rulers governed.

**Boltzmann's entropy formula, S = k ln W**
Ludwig Boltzmann showed that entropy equals Boltzmann's constant times the natural log of the number of microstates (W or Ω). Microstates are the microscopic arrangements consistent with a system's macroscopic state. This "k log W" formula is inscribed on Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna.

**Second law of thermodynamics**
This law states that entropy never decreases in an isolated (closed) system, so the universe's entropy always increases. It is equivalent to Clausius's statement that heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder to a hotter body. Arthur Eddington used it to define the "arrow of time," and its long-term consequence is the "heat death" of the universe.

**Gibbs free energy, G = H − TS**
Gibbs free energy equals enthalpy minus temperature times entropy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant temperature). A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative. An endothermic reaction (positive ΔH) can therefore be spontaneous only if its entropy change is positive and large enough.

**Clausius theorem / Clausius inequality**
Rudolf Clausius defined the change in entropy as the integral of dQ/T (heat transferred divided by temperature) for a reversible process. For any cycle, the integral of dQ/T is less than or equal to zero, with equality for reversible cycles. Equivalently, dS ≥ dQ/T. The reciprocal of temperature, 1/T, is the classic example of an integrating factor: it turns the inexact differential of heat into the exact differential dS.

**Carnot cycle**
This idealized heat engine alternates two isothermal steps (constant temperature) with two adiabatic steps (constant entropy, or isentropic). Because of this, it traces a rectangle on a temperature–entropy diagram. Its entropy bookkeeping shows that no heat engine can be 100% efficient.

**Sackur–Tetrode equation**
This equation gives the absolute entropy of a monatomic ideal gas, and it is properly extensive because it accounts for the indistinguishability of particles. It is valid in the classical regime, where the volume per particle is much larger than the cube of the thermal de Broglie wavelength (V/Nλ³ ≫ 1).

**Gibbs paradox**
This thought experiment by J. Willard Gibbs involves mixing two samples of the same ideal gas. Treating the particles as distinguishable wrongly predicts an entropy of mixing, so entropy seems to change, or even decrease, in ways that violate the second law. The paradox is resolved by treating identical particles as indistinguishable (dividing by N!), which makes entropy extensive.

**Third law of thermodynamics and residual entropy**
The third law says the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero. Non-crystalline or disordered solids, such as ice or geometrically frustrated magnets, keep a nonzero "residual entropy" at absolute zero because they still have multiple possible ground-state configurations.

**Bekenstein–Hawking formula**
Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that a black hole's entropy is proportional to the surface area of its event horizon, not to its volume. Bekenstein also proposed a related upper limit on how much entropy (information) a region of space can contain.

**Shannon entropy**
Claude Shannon's information-theoretic entropy is the expected information content of a random variable, given by −Σ pᵢ log pᵢ. It is the information analogue of the thermodynamic Gibbs entropy. Linking information to entropy is one way the Maxwell's demon paradox is resolved.

**Maxwell's demon**
James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being that opens a door between two gas chambers to sort fast molecules from slow ones. This would lower entropy without doing work, apparently violating the second law. The resolution is that acquiring and erasing information has an entropy cost.

**Helmholtz free energy, A = U − TS**
Helmholtz free energy equals internal energy minus temperature times entropy. It measures the useful work obtainable from a system at constant temperature and volume.

**Von Neumann entropy**
This is the quantum-mechanical version of entropy, defined as S = −Tr(ρ ln ρ), where ρ is the density matrix describing a quantum state. It is zero for a pure state and positive for mixed states.

**Fluctuation theorem**
This result from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics gives the probability that a system's entropy decreases over a given time interval. Such decreases are possible but exponentially less likely than increases of the same size, especially for large systems or long times.

**Clapeyron equation and phase transitions**
The slope of a coexistence curve on a phase diagram is dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV, the entropy change of the transition divided by the volume change. The entropy change in a phase transition equals the latent heat divided by the transition temperature. Trouton's rule notes that the entropy of vaporization is roughly the same, about 85–88 J/(mol·K), for many liquids at their boiling points.

**Carmen (Georges Bizet)**
This opera by Georges Bizet follows Carmen, a fiery cigarette-factory worker in Seville. In the "Habanera" she sings that "love is a rebellious bird," and after being arrested by Zuniga she seduces Don José with a seguidilla. She later turns to the toreador Escamillo, and the jealous Don José stabs her to death at the end.

**War of the Buffoons**
This was a 1750s Parisian pamphlet war, known in French as the Querelle des Bouffons. It began after a performance of Pergolesi's Italian opera buffa *La serva padrona*. Supporters of the native French "tragédie lyrique" (musical tragedy), led by Rameau's partisans, fought supporters of Italian comic opera, who included Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

**French overture**
This Baroque two-part form opens with a slow, stately section in dotted rhythms, followed by a fast fugal section, and both parts are often repeated. Jean-Baptiste Lully developed it, and composers across Europe imitated it. Bach's second *Clavier-Übung* includes an "Overture in the French Style."

**Boléro (Maurice Ravel)**
Dancer Ida Rubinstein commissioned this 1928 orchestral piece from Ravel. A snare drum plays the same ostinato rhythm 169 times underneath one long, steady crescendo. The title comes from the Spanish dance form.

**"Decisive moment" (Henri Cartier-Bresson)**
Cartier-Bresson was a French photojournalist, and "decisive moment" was his term for the instant that captures an event's meaning. His 1932 *Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare* shows a man leaping from a ladder over a puddle behind a Paris train station. He also photographed a crowd rushing a Shanghai bank to buy gold.

**Daguerreotype (Louis Daguerre)**
This was the first commercially successful photographic process, announced in 1839 and named for its inventor, Louis Daguerre. It produced images on silvered plates sensitized with iodine. Daguerre's *Boulevard du Temple* includes a man having his shoes shined, the first person ever photographed. The oldest surviving photograph, Niépce's view from a window at Le Gras, was also taken in France.

**Nadar in a balloon**
Nadar was a pioneering French photographer and balloonist. Honoré Daumier's 1862 lithograph shows him in a hot-air balloon, "elevating photography to the height of art." In the 1860s, Nadar also used artificial light to photograph the catacombs and sewers beneath Paris.

**Jean-Baptiste Lully's death by gangrene**
Lully was the leading composer at Louis XIV's court. In 1687, while conducting a Te Deum, he struck his foot with the heavy staff he used to beat time. The wound turned gangrenous and killed him. With Molière and choreographer Pierre Beauchamp he also pioneered the comédie-ballet.

**Treatise on Harmony (Jean-Philippe Rameau)**
Rameau published this 1722 treatise, which controversially grounded harmony in mathematical and acoustic principles. He was also a major Baroque opera composer. His works include the tragédie lyrique *Hippolyte et Aricie* and the opéra-ballet *Les Indes galantes*, which contains the "Dance of the Peace Pipe."

**The Art of Playing the Harpsichord / Le Tombeau de Couperin**
François Couperin, nicknamed "le Grand," published this 1716 keyboard treatise in Paris. He also wrote harpsichord pieces such as *Les Barricades mystérieuses*, which use the arpeggiated French "broken style" (style brisé). Ravel later honored him in *Le Tombeau de Couperin*, a six-movement piano suite.

**The 400 Blows and Breathless (French New Wave)**
These are the defining films of the 1950s–60s French New Wave. In Truffaut's *The 400 Blows*, the boy Antoine Doinel is accused of plagiarizing Balzac, and the film ends with him running toward the ocean. Godard's *Breathless* uses frequent jump cuts to follow a car thief who idolizes Humphrey Bogart.

**Pavane for a Dead Princess**
Ravel wrote this slow, stately 1899 piano piece and dedicated it to the Princesse de Polignac. Ravel studied with Gabriel Fauré at the Paris Conservatoire, and Fauré also wrote a well-known Pavane in F-sharp minor.

**"Au fond du temple saint" (The Pearl Fishers)**
This "friendship duet" comes from Bizet's 1863 opera *The Pearl Fishers*. In it, Nadir and Zurga recall seeing a beautiful woman in a temple and swear to remain friends.

**Quartet for the End of Time (Olivier Messiaen)**
Messiaen wrote this chamber work while a prisoner of war in a German camp, and it premiered there in 1941. Its movements include "Crystal Liturgy" and "Abyss of the Birds," a long solo for clarinet that reflects his love of birdsong. Messiaen also wrote the *Turangalîla-Symphonie* and theorized "modes of limited transposition."

**Pierre Boulez and IRCAM**
Boulez was a French composer and conductor who wrote *Le Marteau sans maître* (*The Hammer Without a Master*). He founded IRCAM, a Paris institute for contemporary and electronic music, whose new technology premiered in his work *Répons*. The main concert hall of the Philharmonie de Paris is now named for him.

**Langar**
The free communal kitchen found in every gurdwara (Sikh house of worship). Volunteers called sevadars cook simple vegetarian meals and serve them to anyone who comes, whatever their religion, caste, gender or background. Guests traditionally sit together on the floor as equals, and the practice goes back to Guru Nanak.

**Five Ks (kesh, kangha, kara, kirpan, kachera)**
Five articles of faith that initiated Sikhs keep at all times. They are kesh (uncut hair), kangha (a wooden comb), kara (an iron or steel bracelet), kirpan (a dagger) and kachera (cotton undershorts). Male Sikhs usually cover their uncut hair with a turban.

**Kirpan**
The ceremonial dagger or curved blade that is one of the Five Ks. It stands for a Sikh's duty to defend the weak and fight injustice, and it reflects the ideal of the "saint-soldier," someone who is both spiritually devout and ready to fight for what is right.

**Guru Nanak**
The founder of Sikhism and the first of its ten human Gurus, born in Punjab in 1469. He is credited with the saying "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim." Stories about his life are collected in biographies called janamsakhis. In one of them, he falls asleep with his feet pointing toward the Kaaba in Mecca, and when someone turns his feet away, the Kaaba moves to follow them.

**Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth)**
The central scripture of Sikhism, written in the Gurmukhi script. Before he died in 1708, the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, declared that the scripture would be the final and eternal Guru instead of another person. It sits on a raised throne in the gurdwara, and a fan made of yak hair (the chaur) is waved over it as a sign of respect.

**Mul Mantar / Ik Onkar**
The Mul Mantar is the opening verse of the Guru Granth Sahib, often described as a twelve-word statement of belief in one God. It begins the Japji Sahib and starts with the words "Ik Onkar," meaning "One God" or "One Supreme Reality." The Ik Onkar symbol is one of the best-known emblems of Sikhism.

**Gobind Singh and the Khalsa**
Gobind Singh was the tenth and last human Guru of Sikhism. In 1699 he founded the Khalsa, a community of initiated "saint-soldiers" who must follow the Five Ks. He also wrote the Zafarnama ("Epistle of Victory"), a letter to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Male Khalsa members take the surname Singh, and women take Kaur.

**Panj Pyare ("Five Beloved Ones")**
The first five members of the Khalsa. In 1699 Gobind Singh asked a gathering, "I need one head." Five men volunteered one after another, and each went into a tent with him. Each time he came out with a bloody sword, as if he had beheaded the man, but at the end all five came out alive and became the first initiates of the Khalsa.

**Amrit Sanchar (Khanda di Pahul)**
The initiation ceremony, similar to a baptism, by which Sikhs join the Khalsa. Prayers are recited while amrit, a mixture of sugar and water, is stirred with a double-edged sword called the khanda. Initiates drink the amrit, and it is also sprinkled on their eyes and hair. Sikhs who have not taken amrit are called sehajdhari.

**Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib)**
The holiest gurdwara in Sikhism, located in Amritsar, Punjab. Its building is linked to the fourth Guru, Ram Das, who founded Amritsar. Next to it stands the Akal Takht, the highest seat of Sikh religious authority.

**Gurdwara**
The Sikh house of worship, a name meaning "doorway to the Guru." People of every faith are welcome. Inside, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are sung and karah prasad, a sweet brown pudding, is handed out to the congregation. A tall triangular flag called the Nishan Sahib flies outside.

**Five Thieves**
The five vices that Sikhism teaches believers to overcome: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They are called "thieves" because they rob a person of good judgment and keep the soul from union with God.

**Naam Japo and the Three Pillars**
Naam Japo, meditating on and repeating God's name, is one of the Three Pillars of Sikh life. The other two are Kirat Karo, earning an honest living, and Vand Chakko, sharing what you have with others, including giving part of your income to charity. In Sikhism, God is also called Akal Purakh, "the Timeless Being."

**Khanda symbol and Miri-Piri**
The Khanda is the main emblem of Sikhism. It shows a double-edged sword in the middle of a circular weapon called a chakkar, with two kirpans curving around them. The two kirpans stand for Miri-Piri, the idea of holding both worldly and spiritual authority. The sixth Guru, Hargobind, introduced this idea after his father, Guru Arjan, was tortured and executed by the Mughals, which included being made to sit on a hot iron plate. The Khanda appears on the Nishan Sahib flag.

**Naam Karan**
The Sikh naming ceremony for a newborn. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the child's name is chosen to begin with the first letter of the hymn on that page.

**Halahala poison and Nilakantha ("blue throat")**
When the gods and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk (the Samudra Manthan) to get the nectar of immortality, a deadly poison called halahala came up and threatened to destroy the world. Shiva drank it to save creation, and it turned his throat blue. This earned him the epithet Nilakantha ("blue-throated"). In some versions, his wife Parvati grabbed his throat so the poison would not reach his stomach.

**Nataraja, the "Lord of the Dance"**
In this form, Shiva is the cosmic dancer. He performs the Tandava, a dance that destroys and recreates the universe, and Parvati's gentler counterpart dance is the Lasya. Classic bronze statues show him inside a ring of flames, holding a small drum (the damaru) whose beat sets the rhythm of creation.

**Beheading of Ganesha**
Parvati created a son to guard her chamber. When the boy blocked Shiva from entering, Shiva cut off his head in anger. To calm the grieving Parvati, the boy was brought back to life with an elephant's head, and he became the elephant-headed god Ganesha.

**Trimurti and "The Destroyer"**
Hinduism's divine triad, the Trimurti, is made up of Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, and Shiva the destroyer. Shiva's destruction is seen as necessary so that the universe can be renewed and created again.

**Sati, Daksha, and Parvati**
Shiva's first wife, Sati, was the daughter of Daksha Prajapati. Daksha insulted Shiva and left him out of a great sacrificial ritual (a yajna), so Sati burned herself to death in the sacrificial fire. In his rage, Shiva had Daksha beheaded, which is why he has been compared to the wild Greek god Dionysus. Sati was later reborn as Parvati, who became Shiva's wife again.

**Nandi**
Nandi is the white bull that Shiva rides and that serves as his gatekeeper. Statues of Nandi usually sit in Shiva temples, facing the main shrine.

**Mount Kailash and Ravana**
Shiva lives with his family on Mount Kailash (Kailasa) in the Himalayas. The demon king Ravana tried to lift or uproot the mountain, and Shiva pinned him under it by pressing down with his toe. Ravana sang Shiva's praises until he was released, and Shiva rewarded his devotion with the sword Chandrahasa.

**Third eye and the burning of Kama**
Shiva has a third eye on his forehead that can burn things to ash, which is why he is called Tryambakam ("three-eyed"). The gods needed Shiva to father a son who could kill the demon Tarakasura, so the love god Kama (Kamadeva) shot him with a love arrow while he meditated. Shiva burned Kama to ashes with his third eye. Kalidasa tells this story in the poem *Kumarasambhava*.

**Ganga flowing from his hair**
Shiva has matted hair and wears a crescent moon on his head. When the river goddess Ganga came down from heaven, Shiva caught her in his hair so her force would not destroy the Earth. Art often shows the Ganges River flowing out of his locks.

**Lingam**
Shiva is most often worshipped through the lingam, a phallic or column-shaped symbol that represents him without showing a human figure. Worshippers place offerings on it, such as water, milk, and bael (bilva) leaves.

**Pillar of fire and the beheading of Brahma**
Brahma and Vishnu argued over which of them was greater, and Shiva appeared between them as an endless pillar of fire. Vishnu became a boar and dug down to find its bottom, while Brahma became a swan (gander) and flew up to find its top. Brahma lied that he had reached the top, so Shiva, sometimes in his fierce form Bhairava, cut off one of Brahma's five heads.

**Apasmara**
Apasmara is a dwarf who stands for ignorance. Shiva crushes him under his foot as Nataraja, which symbolizes the defeat of ignorance.

**Ardhanarishvara**
In this combined form, Shiva and Parvati appear as one deity who is half male and half female. Shiva usually makes up the right half and Parvati the left. The form shows that male and female principles depend on each other.

**Kartikeya and the race around the world**
Kartikeya (also called Skanda or Murugan) is Shiva's other son with Parvati, born to defeat the demon Taraka. Shiva set a contest between his two sons to race around the world for a magic mango. Kartikeya set off around the world, but Ganesha won by walking around his parents, saying that they were his whole world.

**Vibhuti and Maha Shivaratri**
Shiva is often shown covered in ash, and his devotees draw three horizontal lines of white ash (vibhuti) across their foreheads. During his festival, Maha Shivaratri ("Great Night of Shiva"), worshippers offer bilva leaves. The custom recalls a hunter who hid in a bilva tree all night and kept dropping leaves onto a lingam below.

**Categorical imperative**
This is Kant's supreme principle of morality. It tells you to "act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law." It is "categorical" because it binds everyone unconditionally, regardless of their desires. A "hypothetical" imperative, by contrast, only applies if you want a certain goal. It is the core of Kant's deontological (duty-based) ethics.

**Critique of Pure Reason**
Kant's most famous work, first published in 1781, is the first of his three "Critiques." The other two are the Critique of Practical Reason and the Critique of Judgment. It asks what reason can know independently of experience. Its answer is that the mind actively structures experience but cannot know reality as it is in itself.

**Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals**
This 1785 work is Kant's short foundational book on ethics, also translated as "Grounding" or "Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals." It argues that the only thing good without qualification is a "good will," meaning a will that acts from duty. It then derives the categorical imperative. His later Metaphysics of Morals, divided into a "Doctrine of Right" and a "Doctrine of Virtue," expands on it.

**Lying to the murderer at the door (reply to Benjamin Constant)**
The French thinker Benjamin Constant objected to Kant's ethics. He argued that it would forbid lying even to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding. In his essay "On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy," Kant accepted this conclusion. He held that lying is always wrong and that you cannot justify a lie by its expected outcomes.

**Noumenon / "thing-in-itself" vs. phenomena**
Kant distinguished phenomena, things as they appear to us through our senses and mental structures, from noumena or "things-in-themselves," reality as it exists independently of us. We can know phenomena but never the thing-in-itself. Schopenhauer later argued that Kant had changed the earlier meaning of "noumenon."

**Synthetic a priori judgments ("7 + 5 = 12")**
Kant separated "analytic" judgments, which are true by definition, from "synthetic" judgments, which add new information. He also separated "a priori" knowledge, known independently of experience (literally "from the earlier"), from a posteriori knowledge, known from experience. His central claim is that synthetic a priori truths exist, and he used the arithmetic statement "7 + 5 = 12" and geometry as his examples.

**Kingdom of Ends**
This is Kant's ideal of a community in which every rational being is both a lawmaker and subject to the moral laws it makes. Each member treats all the others as ends, never as mere tools. It is the basis of one of the formulations of the categorical imperative.

**"What is Enlightenment?" ("Sapere aude")**
In this 1784 essay Kant defines Enlightenment as "man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity," meaning the inability to use one's own understanding without someone else's guidance. Its motto is the Latin "Sapere aude," which means "Dare to know." The essay also argues that "the public use of one's reason must be free at all times."

**Transcendental idealism and the "Copernican revolution"**
Kant's theory of knowledge holds that space and time are forms built into our perception, not features of things-in-themselves. On this view the world we experience is shaped by the mind's own rules. He compared this to Copernicus's revolution: instead of our knowledge conforming to objects, objects must conform to our ways of knowing. This is why some things can be known a priori.

**"Dogmatic slumber" (David Hume)**
In the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics, Kant wrote that reading the Scottish skeptic David Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber." Hume's attack on the idea of causation pushed Kant to work out how necessary, synthetic a priori knowledge is possible.

**Perfect and imperfect duties**
Kant divided moral duties into perfect duties and imperfect duties. Perfect duties must always be obeyed, such as never lying or never making false promises. Imperfect duties must be pursued but allow some flexibility in how and when, such as developing your talents or helping others. Each kind applies to oneself and to others, and his four examples are often shown in a four-square grid.

**Formula of Humanity ("end in itself")**
This formulation of the categorical imperative says to "act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, never merely as a means, but always at the same time as an end." It rests on Kant's view that rational, self-governing beings have dignity; he wrote that "humanity itself is a dignity." Other formulations include those of universal law, autonomy, and the Kingdom of Ends.

**Categories of understanding**
In the Critique of Pure Reason, Kant reworked Aristotle's categories into twelve pure concepts of the understanding, which he derived from a "table of judgments." They fall into four groups (quantity, quality, relation, and modality), and the mind must use them to organize any experience. "Schemata" link these pure concepts to what we perceive through the senses.

**Arthur Schopenhauer's critique**
Schopenhauer was a German philosopher strongly influenced by Kant. He wrote a "Critique of the Kantian Philosophy" as an appendix to The World as Will and Representation. He also attacked Kant's ethics in his essay "On the Basis of Morality."

**Critique of Judgment (aesthetics)**
Kant's third Critique deals with aesthetic and teleological judgment. It contrasts the "agreeable" (e.g., "this steak is good") with the beautiful, which pleases "without interest," and with the sublime. It also says that through genius "nature gives the rule to art." Nietzsche mocked the "disinterested" view of beauty in On the Genealogy of Morals.

**The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money**
Keynes's 1936 masterpiece and the founding text of modern macroeconomics. It argued that aggregate demand, not supply, determines output and employment. It treated full employment as only a "special case," and it introduced liquidity preference and the "marginal efficiency of capital."

**The Economic Consequences of the Peace**
Keynes's 1919 attack on the Treaty of Versailles, which made him famous. He had served as a British Treasury representative at the Paris Peace Conference and resigned in protest. He then wrote this book, arguing that heavy reparations on Germany would be economically disastrous. He blamed figures such as the "Heavenly Twins," Lords Cunliffe and Sumner, who demanded "astronomical" reparations.

**Deficit spending to fight the Great Depression**
Keynes argued that governments should spend more, even if it means running deficits, when private demand collapses during a recession. Such countercyclical fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand to the right and reduces unemployment. His ideas are often contrasted with supply-side economics, and he is linked to Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal era.

**Keynesian cross**
A diagram that plots aggregate expenditure (demand) against national income or output. Equilibrium GDP occurs where the expenditure curve, built from the consumption function, crosses a 45-degree line where output equals spending. The cross can be used to derive the IS curve.

**"In the long run, we are all dead"**
Keynes's famous quip from A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923). It mocks economists who claim markets will self-correct "in the long run" while ignoring present suffering. The same book discusses the quantity theory of money and argues that deflation is worse than currency depreciation.

**Beauty contest**
An analogy from The General Theory for financial markets. Judges are rewarded for picking the faces others will find prettiest, not the ones they personally prefer. Investors therefore try to guess "what average opinion expects the average opinion to be," reaching "the third degree" and beyond. The analogy challenges the idea that prices reflect fundamentals.

**IS-LM model**
A model created by John Hicks in his paper "Mr. Keynes and the Classics" and expanded by Alvin Hansen to summarize the General Theory. It plots the IS (investment-saving) curve against the LM (liquidity-money) curve. A horizontal LM curve represents a "liquidity trap," where monetary policy cannot lower interest rates further.

**"Carthaginian peace"**
Keynes's term for the Treaty of Versailles. It compares the treaty to Rome's total destruction of Carthage and implies the treaty aimed to crush Germany economically. Étienne Mantoux later rebutted Keynes in The Carthaginian Peace, or the Economic Consequences of Mr. Keynes.

**Rejection of Say's law**
Say's law is the classical claim that "supply creates its own demand." Keynes rejected it, arguing that demand can fall short and leave an economy stuck with high unemployment. He also attacked the law in works such as The Means to Prosperity.

**A Treatise on Probability**
Keynes's 1921 philosophical work defending a "logical-relationist" view of probability. In it, he describes deciding whether to carry an umbrella in case of rain as an example of "irreducible uncertainty" that cannot be precisely quantified.

**Multiplier effect**
The idea that an initial increase in government spending or investment raises national income by more than the original amount, because each round of spending becomes someone else's income. The size of the multiplier depends on the marginal propensity to consume.

**"Animal spirits"**
Keynes's phrase, borrowed from older Cartesian usage, for the spontaneous urge to act that drives investment decisions instead of careful calculation of risk. He used it to explain why long-run expectations, and therefore business investment, are unstable.

**Bancor and the Bretton Woods Conference**
At Bretton Woods in 1944, Keynes proposed an International Clearing Union with a supranational currency called the "bancor" to settle trade imbalances between nations. E. F. Schumacher's paper "Multilateral Clearing" influenced the idea. The proposal was not adopted, but Keynes helped shape the IMF and the World Bank.

**Indian Currency and Finance**
Keynes's first book, published in 1913, analyzing India's monetary system and the gold-exchange standard. It discusses the problems of tying the rupee to gold. Keynes also served on the Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency, known as the Chamberlain Commission.

**Sticky prices and New Keynesian economics**
Keynes argued that wages and prices adjust slowly ("stickily") to shocks, so markets do not clear quickly and unemployment can persist. The later New Keynesian school formalizes this nominal rigidity using tools such as the Calvo staggered-pricing model.

**George Floyd's death in Minneapolis**
George Floyd was a Black man killed by Minneapolis police on May 25, 2020, after a Cup Foods employee reported that he had used a counterfeit twenty-dollar bill. While being pinned down, he repeatedly said "I can't breathe." His death set off nationwide protests in summer 2020. A raised-fist sculpture by Jordan Powell-Karis was later placed at his memorial site.

**Derek Chauvin**
Chauvin is the Minneapolis police officer who knelt on Floyd's neck. He was convicted of murder in April 2021 in a trial overseen by Judge Peter Cahill. Witnesses included bystander Genevieve Hansen and defense use-of-force expert Barry Brodd. Fellow officers J. Alexander Kueng and Tou Thao were tried separately for their roles.

**Tim Walz**
Walz has been Minnesota's Democratic governor since 2019 and governs from the capital, St. Paul. He handled the state's response to Floyd's death. In 2024 he was Kamala Harris's vice-presidential running mate, and he became known for calling J.D. Vance and Republicans "weird."

**Ilhan Omar**
Omar is a Somali-born former refugee who has represented a Minneapolis-based district in the U.S. House since 2019. Minnesota has the largest Somali-American population in the country. She is a member of the progressive "Squad" and has twice beaten former Minneapolis city council member Don Samuels in Democratic primaries, including in 2024.

**Amy Klobuchar**
Klobuchar is Minnesota's senior U.S. senator and ran for president in 2020. That campaign drew controversy over reports that she mistreated her Senate staff. In 2022 she pulled back her own Journalism Competition and Preservation Act after Ted Cruz got an amendment added to it.

**"Some people did something"**
Ilhan Omar used this phrase about the 9/11 attacks in a 2019 speech to the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR). Critics said it played down the attacks, and it caused a major controversy.

**8 minutes and 46 seconds / Blackout Tuesday**
This was the length of time Chauvin was first reported to have knelt on Floyd's neck, and it became a national symbol of protest against racism and police brutality. Walz declared a moment of silence of that length on Blackout Tuesday (June 2, 2020), a day of social-media protest in which people posted black squares.

**Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL)**
The DFL is Minnesota's branch of the Democratic Party. It was formed in 1944 when the state Democratic Party merged with the Farmer-Labor Party. Collin Peterson, a longtime DFL congressman, lost his seat to Republican Michelle Fischbach in 2020.

**Tim Pawlenty**
Pawlenty was Minnesota's Republican governor from 2003 to 2011. He tried to return to the office in 2018 to succeed Mark Dayton but lost the Republican primary.

**Mark Dayton**
Dayton was Minnesota's DFL governor from 2011 to 2019, having defeated Republican Tom Emmer in a close 2010 race. In 2018 he appointed his lieutenant governor, Tina Smith, to the U.S. Senate seat that Al Franken gave up. Smith then won the 2018 special election against Karin Housley.

**St. Paul and the Twin Cities**
St. Paul is Minnesota's capital. Together with neighboring Minneapolis, the state's largest city, it forms the "Twin Cities." Suburbs in the metro area include Brooklyn Center.

**"It's all about the Benjamins, baby"**
Omar posted this in 2019 to suggest that the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC buys political support ("Benjamins" are $100 bills). Many condemned it as an antisemitic trope, and she apologized. Republicans cited it in 2023 when they removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

**Darnella Frazier**
Frazier was 17 when she filmed the bystander video of Floyd's killing that spread around the world. She received a PEN America courage award and a special Pulitzer citation, and she testified at Chauvin's trial.

**Daunte Wright**
Wright was a 20-year-old Black man shot dead in April 2021 in Brooklyn Center, while Chauvin's trial was going on nearby. Officer Kim Potter said she meant to draw her Taser but fired her gun by mistake. She was later convicted of manslaughter.

**Al Franken**
Franken, a former *Saturday Night Live* comedian, won a 2008 Senate race against Republican Norm Coleman that was so close it took months of recounts and legal challenges before Coleman conceded. Franken resigned in 2018 after allegations of sexual misconduct.

**Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira**
These are Kilimanjaro's three volcanic cones. Kibo is the highest and youngest, and it is dormant rather than extinct. Mawenzi is a jagged, eroded peak with sub-peaks such as Neumann Tower. Shira is a worn-down cone that formed the broad Shira Plateau. Together they make Kilimanjaro a stratovolcano and the tallest freestanding mountain in the world, meaning it is not part of a range.

**Uhuru Peak ("Freedom Peak")**
Uhuru Peak is the summit of Kilimanjaro, on the rim of Kibo's crater. At about 5,895 m (19,341 ft) it is the highest point in Africa. The name means "freedom" in Swahili, and the peak was renamed after Tanganyika became independent in 1961. Some questions call the whole mountain "Uhuru."

**Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller**
German geographer Hans Meyer and Austrian climber Ludwig Purtscheller made the first recorded ascent to the summit in 1889. Meyer is the name questions mention most often for the first climb.

**Barranco Wall**
The Barranco Wall, also called the Great Barranco Wall, is a steep cliff of rock and ancient lava below Kibo's southern face. Climbers on the popular Machame and Lemosho routes have to scramble up it. Several questions also mention the Lava Tower, a volcanic rock formation near the Barranco area.

**Moshi**
Moshi is the town on Kilimanjaro's southern slopes and the main starting point for climbs. It serves as the gateway to Kilimanjaro National Park. Mount Meru, Tanzania's second-highest mountain, lies to the west, and Mount Kenya is about 200 miles to the north.

**Chagga people**
The Chagga are a Bantu-speaking people who have long farmed the fertile southern and eastern slopes of Kilimanjaro, growing crops such as bananas and coffee. Their traditions link their chief god to the mountain. One theory says the name "Kilimanjaro" comes from a misunderstood Chagga phrase saying the mountain could not be climbed.

**Furtwängler Glacier**
The Furtwängler Glacier is a small glacier near the summit on Kibo's ice cap. Like the rest of Kilimanjaro's ice, it has shrunk sharply in recent decades and may disappear entirely, which makes it a common example of glacial retreat in Africa.

**Johannes Rebmann (Rebmann Glacier)**
Johannes Rebmann was a German missionary who in 1848 became the first European to report snow on Kilimanjaro, describing its "dazzling whiteness." Many geographers in Europe doubted that snow could exist so close to the equator. The Rebmann Glacier on Kibo's southern face is named for him, and the Decken and Kersten Glaciers lie near it.

**Western Breach**
The Western Breach is a large gap in the western rim of Kibo's crater, formed by a landslide or collapse. It is a steep, difficult route to the summit. It is reached from near the Arrow Glacier and the Lava Tower, and the Lemosho Route leads toward it.

**Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze**
Hans Meyer named the summit Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze (Kaiser Wilhelm Peak) when the area was part of German East Africa. Kilimanjaro sat on the border between British and German East Africa, on the German side. A popular story says Queen Victoria gave the mountain to her grandson Wilhelm II as a gift, but this has been shown to be a myth.

**Saddle Plateau**
The Saddle is a high, desert-like plateau that separates Kibo's snow-capped cone from Mawenzi's jagged peak. Climbers on the eastern routes cross it on the way to Kibo.

**Garden of Senecios**
The Garden of Senecios is an area on the climbing routes named for Kilimanjaro's giant groundsels. These are tall, tree-like plants such as *Dendrosenecio kilimanjari* that store water in their leaf rosettes. They grow only in the high mountains of East Africa, and they are among Kilimanjaro's best-known plants.

**Gilman's Point and Stella Point**
Gilman's Point and Stella Point are two points on the rim of Kibo's crater where climbers often stop before the final walk along the rim to Uhuru Peak. Gilman's Point is reached by the eastern routes, and Stella Point by the southern routes.

**Reusch Crater**
The Reusch Crater is an inner volcanic crater inside Kibo's caldera, named for the Lutheran missionary Richard Reusch. The Ash Pit, a deeper volcanic vent, lies inside it.

**Machame and Lemosho Routes**
Machame is the most popular climbing route. Lemosho approaches from the west across the Shira Plateau, and both routes pass the Barranco Wall. The Mweka route is often used for the descent.
